forbidden_claims.statement_nl: Let $n$ be an integer greater than 1. For which real numbers $x$ is \\[\\lfloor nx \\rfloor - \\sum_{k=1}^{n} \\frac{\\lfloor kx \\rfloor}{k}\\] maximal, and what is the maximal value that this expression can take?

payload.previous_feedback: Previous vetter reason: The proof matches the lemma exactly: it defines m = floor(x), sets f = x - m = frac(x), proves 0 <= f < 1 from the floor property, and concludes x = floor(x) + frac(x). No semantic drift or dependency issue is present.
payload.previous_proof_nl: Let x be any real number. Set m = floor(x). By the defining property of the floor function, m is an integer with m <= x < m + 1. Define f = x - m. Then f >= 0, since x >= m, and f < 1, since x < m + 1. By the standard definition of the fractional part, frac(x) = x - floor(x) = x - m = f. Therefore x = m + f = floor(x) + frac(x), and also 0 <= frac(x) < 1. Since x was arbitrary, the statement holds for every real number x.

result_payload.proof_nl: Let x be any real number, and set m = floor(x). By the defining property of the floor function, m is an integer such that m <= x < m + 1. Subtracting m from all parts gives 0 <= x - m < 1. By the definition of the fractional part, frac(x) = x - floor(x) = x - m. Therefore 0 <= frac(x) < 1, and also x = floor(x) + frac(x). Since x was arbitrary, the statement holds for every real number x.
result_payload.proof_summary: Use m = floor(x). The floor property gives m <= x < m+1, so x-m lies in [0,1). By definition, x-m = frac(x), hence x = floor(x) + frac(x) and 0 <= frac(x) < 1.
